title: 괜찮아요 does NOT mean "yes" 😅 #learnkorean
caption:
When someone offers you something in Korean, 괜찮아요 usually means "No, thanks."

괜찮아요 (gwaen-cha-na-yo) = No, thanks (when you're offered something)
네, 좋아요! (ne, jo-a-yo) = Yes, please!
네, 주세요 (ne, ju-se-yo) works too.

괜찮아요 can also mean "I'm okay / it's fine" — but as an answer to "Want a bite?", it's a polite no.
The snack is 붕어빵 (bung-eo-ppang), a fish-shaped pastry Koreans love in autumn and winter 🐟

pinnedComment: Has 괜찮아요 ever cost YOU something? 👇
alt: A needle-felted autumn park with golden ginkgo leaves. A felt young man on a bench offers the last fish-shaped pastry to a coral felt mascot: 한 입 먹을래? (Want a bite?) The mascot really wants it and happily says 괜찮아요! He answers 아, 괜찮아? 알았어! (Oh, no thanks? Okay!) and eats it. The mascot, stretched toward the pastry, freezes and goes pale; he heard No, thanks. It deflates next to the empty paper bag. When someone offers, 괜찮아요 means No, thanks. To accept, say 네, 좋아요! (Yes, please!) The mascot practices in a whisper. He comes back with a new pastry, asks again, and the mascot instantly shouts 네, 좋아요! and hugs it. He asks 나도 한 입만… (Can I have one bite…?) and his hand freezes in mid-air as the mascot turns away.
